rationale.subject: OSPF reference bandwidth
rationale.justification: The default 100 Mbps reference gives FastEthernet, 1G and 10G links the same cost (1). Raising it to 100 Gbps makes cost = 100000 / link Mbps, so 10G = 10, 1G = 100 and SPF prefers the faster path. Must be identical on every router.

rationale.subject: Cloud boundary
rationale.justification: The cloud VPC is a separate administrative and routing domain; cloud VPN gateways only exchange dynamic routes via BGP. eBGP isolates the domains: the enterprise advertises one aggregate (10.64.0.0/16) filtered by prefix-list, and accepts only the VPC CIDR, so a mistake on either side cannot leak or black-hole the other's routes. rationale.subject: BGP -> OSPF
rationale.decision: Redistribute VPC prefix into OSPF at NYC
rationale.justification: Spokes keep a local Internet default route (split tunnelling), so the VPC prefix must be injected into OSPF as an E2 route by the hub that terminates the eBGP session; a route-map limits redistribution to the VPC CIDR only.

rationale.subject: Path latency
rationale.decision: Worst path SINGAPORE -> NYC -> CLOUD-VPC = 107.776 ms one-way
rationale.justification: Estimated from cable/route distance at ~4.9 us/km (Internet paths x1.4) plus 0.05 ms per hop. Intercontinental latency is dominated by physics, so chatty IoT protocols should batch telemetry and use MQTT/HTTPS keep-alives rather than synchronous request/response.

rationale.subject: Packet-flow simulation
rationale.justification: Every LAN's last usable address was resolved by longest-prefix match to exactly one subnet (proves zero overlap), and representative flows (DHCP, DNS, Internet, lateral SMB, cloud MQTT/SSH) were walked through each generated ACL entry-by-entry using the same wildcard arithmetic the router applies.

      Why: Public WAN addresses in the lab use the RFC 5737 documentation block so the configs never collide with real Internet space; replace with ISP-assigned addresses in production.

== L3 Routing ============================================================
[039] Interior gateway protocol: Multi-area OSPFv2 (area 0 backbone at NYC, one area per remote site)
      Why: Selected multi-area OSPF because 4 geographically dispersed sites interconnect over an Internet/IPsec WAN whose tunnels can flap independently. Areas confine Type-1/2 LSA flooding and SPF recalculation to the site where a change happens; area 0 carries only inter-area summaries. OSPF remains vendor-neutral and converges in seconds as a link-state protocol.
      Ref: RFC 2328 (OSPFv2) section 3, RFC 3509 (ABR behaviour)
[040] Area 1 summary (LONDON): area 1 range 10.64.8.0 255.255.252.0
      Why: The ABR at LONDON advertises 3 intra-area subnets into area 0 as one Type-3 LSA 10.64.8.0/22. This works only because the VLSM engine allocated the site as one contiguous, bit-aligned block; it shrinks every other router's routing table and hides intra-site flaps from the backbone.
      Ref: RFC 2328 section 12.4.3, RFC 4632
[041] Area 2 summary (SINGAPORE): area 2 range 10.64.12.0 255.255.252.0
      Why: The ABR at SINGAPORE advertises 3 intra-area subnets into area 0 as one Type-3 LSA 10.64.12.0/22. This works only because the VLSM engine allocated the site as one contiguous, bit-aligned block; it shrinks every other router's routing table and hides intra-site flaps from the backbone.
      Ref: RFC 2328 section 12.4.3, RFC 4632
[042] Area 3 summary (MUMBAI): area 3 range 10.64.16.0 255.255.252.0
      Why: The ABR at MUMBAI advertises 3 intra-area subnets into area 0 as one Type-3 LSA 10.64.16.0/22. This works only because the VLSM engine allocated the site as one contiguous, bit-aligned block; it shrinks every other router's routing table and hides intra-site flaps from the backbone.
      Ref: RFC 2328 section 12.4.3, RFC 4632
[043] OSPF reference bandwidth: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100000
      Why: The default 100 Mbps reference gives FastEthernet, 1G and 10G links the same cost (1). Raising it to 100 Gbps makes cost = 100000 / link Mbps, so 10G = 10, 1G = 100 and SPF prefers the faster path. Must be identical on every router.
      Ref: RFC 2328 Appendix C.3
[044] Cloud boundary: eBGP AS65010 <-> AS64512 (CLOUD-VPC)
      Why: The cloud VPC is a separate administrative and routing domain; cloud VPN gateways only exchange dynamic routes via BGP. eBGP isolates the domains: the enterprise advertises one aggregate (10.64.0.0/16) filtered by prefix-list, and accepts only the VPC CIDR, so a mistake on either side cannot leak or black-hole the other's routes. Private ASNs from 64512-65534 are used.
      Ref: RFC 4271 (BGP-4), RFC 6996 (private ASNs), RFC 7454 (BGP filtering)
[045] BGP -> OSPF: Redistribute VPC prefix into OSPF at NYC
      Why: Spokes keep a local Internet default route (split tunnelling), so the VPC prefix must be injected into OSPF as an E2 route by the hub that terminates the eBGP session; a route-map limits redistribution to the VPC CIDR only.
      Ref: RFC 2328 section 2.3 (AS-external routes)
